The model got AGI right ($31,402) but used a sunset-regime deduction stack — a $16,600 basic standard deduction plus $10,600 of personal exemptions — when OBBBA permanently set the 2026 joint standard deduction at $32,200 and kept the personal exemption at $0. Its $28,350 total deduction is roughly $19,000 short of the correct $47,500 stack ($32,200 + $3,300 age-65 additions + $12,000 of senior deductions), and the $3,052 of taxable income it taxed at 10% does not exist against AGI of $31,402.

The model built a $29,600 deduction from a $19,600 standard deduction (age-65 additions included) plus $10,000 of personal exemptions, which is the pre-TCJA regime; the 2026 joint standard deduction alone is $32,200 before the $3,300 of age-65 additions and the $6,000-per-senior OBBBA deduction, and personal exemptions are zero. Its $1,802 of taxable income is exactly the gap created by understating the standard deduction by about $12,600 and adding back exemptions that do not exist in 2026.

The model made two compounding errors: it applied the 85% Social Security inclusion tier to combined income of $36,677, including $11,588 of benefits, when income between the $32,000 and $44,000 joint base amounts includes only the lesser of 50% of the excess over $32,000 ($2,338) or 50% of benefits; and it used a sunset-style $20,400 standard deduction instead of the 2026 joint $32,200 plus $3,300 of age-65 additions plus $12,000 of OBBBA senior deductions. Correct inclusion gives AGI of $31,402, which the basic standard deduction alone exceeds, so its $20,252 of taxable income and $2,025 of tax are entirely artifacts of the over-included benefits and the understated deduction.

The model named the correct SSI-related aged pathway but asserted rather than computed the SSI income test: applying the $20 general exclusion, the $65 earned-income exclusion, and the one-half earned-income disregard gives countable income of about $15,205 from Social Security plus about $14,500 from wages, roughly $2,475 per month, far above the couple SSI federal benefit rate and above Virginia's ~80% FPL aged/blind/disabled limit, which is why SSI received is 0 and medicaid_category is NONE. It compounded this by treating Medicare Savings Program status (QMB/SLMB) and medically needy spend-down as Medicaid-eligibility categories, neither of which is a qualifying pathway here, and by never noticing that household income at 2.05x FPL exceeds even the 100% FPL QMB test.

The model invented a rule that PolicyEngine's aged category is age-only with no income test; the aged/disabled pathway is SSI-linked and requires passing both the SSI income and asset tests, which this household fails with $44,289 of combined wages and Social Security. Because SSI is 0, no category attaches and medicaid_category resolves to NONE despite the head being 71.

The model supplied no rule at all and defaulted age 71 to Medicaid eligibility. Age 71 removes the head from the MAGI expansion adult group (which ends at 64) and routes eligibility to the SSI-linked aged pathway, whose income and asset tests this household fails, so the correct derivation yields no qualifying category; the model's answer is consistent with an age-alone heuristic that skips every income test.

The model equated Medicare Savings Program status with Medicaid eligibility, concluding the head qualifies "as a Medicare savings program recipient"; MSP buy-in is not a PolicyEngine Medicaid eligibility category, and the head qualifies through none of the actual pathways. It also mischaracterized $44,289 of combined wages and Social Security as low income when that is 2.05x FPL, above both the MAGI thresholds and the 100% FPL QMB limit it implicitly relied on.

The model incorrectly treated reaching full retirement age as an exemption from employee Social Security and Medicare taxes. Wages remain subject to FICA regardless of retirement age, producing $1,801.97 of Social Security tax and $421.43 of Medicare tax.

It also treated the mortgage balance as though it established deductible shelter expenses, even though no rent, mortgage payment, property tax, insurance, or utility expense was listed; the $44,289 gross income instead fails the threshold and yields value = 0.

The model correctly computed that the $44,289 household MAGI exceeds 138% FPL for a couple, then overrode its own finding by asserting an aged pathway that tests the spouse's individual income ('spouse with no own income may qualify'). The SSI-related aged/blind/disabled test counts the couple's combined countable income under spousal deeming, not the spouse's zero personal earnings, and Virginia's ABD standard of roughly 80% FPL (about $17,300 for two) is failed by $44,289 by a factor of 2.5; with $0 SSI received, the SSI-recipient route is closed as well.

The model identified the correct pathway, Virginia's aged/blind/disabled category, but misstated its income limit, claiming $15,225 of Social Security plus $29,064 of wages sits 'well under the ABD income and resource limits for a couple after standard disregards.' Virginia's ABD categorically needy standard is about 80% FPL (roughly $17,300 annually for a couple), and the SSI disregards ($20 general, $65 plus half the remainder on earnings) still leave about $29,100 of countable annual income, so the couple fails the income test by more than $10,000; the resource check the model relied on is irrelevant once income disqualifies.

The model invented a rule, asserting that PolicyEngine places everyone 65+ in an 'aged eligibility category, which carries no income test.' No Medicaid category is conferred by age alone: the 65+ non-MAGI route requires SSI receipt or countable income within the state's SSI-related ABD standard (about 80% FPL) plus the $3,000 couple resource limit, and with $0 SSI and $44,289 of household income the engine assigns medicaid_category = NONE.

The model applied no eligibility test at all, defaulting a 69-year-old to 'potentially eligible' on age alone. Running the actual tests yields ineligibility on both branches: age 69 falls outside the 19-64 expansion adult group and the MAGI of 2.05x FPL exceeds the 138% FPL ceiling, while the non-MAGI aged route fails because SSI received is $0 and $44,289 of couple income is far above Virginia's roughly 80% FPL ABD standard.

The model conflated the Medicare Savings Programs with Medicaid eligibility, reasoning that the spouse 'qualifies for Medicaid as Medicare savings program recipient in Virginia.' MSP premium assistance is not a Medicaid eligibility category here, and the household fails it regardless: the QMB limit is 100% FPL while this couple sits at 2.05x FPL. The model also called the 69-year-old 'eligible for Medicare soon' when Medicare eligibility attached at 65, and it never applied any income test to the actual aged/blind/disabled pathway.

The model incorrectly treated 40 quarters of Medicare-covered employment as a prerequisite for Medicare eligibility rather than a condition for premium-free Part A. Under the requested PolicyEngine rule, the spouse's age of 69 satisfies the age-65 Medicare eligibility criterion, so the unlisted work history does not change the result.
